lesson.title: Kalender III: November, Dezember, Feiertag, Ostern, Wochentag
lesson.subtitle: the count closes at ten — and the holiday words walk in with it

hook.title: The Count Closes, the Parties Begin
hook.content: The last two months finish the count the Romans started. November is Latin novem, 'nine', and Dezember is decem, 'ten' — and decem is your old friend wearing Latin clothes: the same ancient word as German zehn and English ten. But Dezember's z is not the shift at work — it is simply how German spells the Latin c, the same writing habit as Zentrum; the shift's own T→Z work lives in zehn. The Roman count still sits inside the name. Then the calendar stops counting and starts celebrating. Der Feiertag is feiern + Tag — a day for celebrating — and Tag is the same ancient word as English day. Der Wochentag is Woche + Tag, the build that runs the whole week: Montag, Dienstag, Freitag — each one is a Wochentag. And then Ostern, the one holiday whose name English also kept: Ostern and Easter are the same Germanic name, built on *aust-, 'dawn, east' — the season when the light comes back. One name, two languages, and neither ever let it go.

footnotes.title: Bede's Honest Doubt
footnotes.content: Everything we know about the goddess behind the name comes from one English monk, Bede, writing in 725: the English, he says, named the spring month after a goddess called Ēostre. Scholars still argue whether she was a real goddess or Bede's own guess from the month's name. What is certain: German Ostern and English Easter are the same name from the same root — *aust-, 'dawn, east' — and the fact that both languages kept it is the aha.

pattern.title: Holidays, Weekdays, the Last Two Months
pattern.content: 1. The months: im November, im Dezember — same masculine frame. 2. The holiday: Heute ist ein Feiertag. 3. The weekday: Der Montag ist ein Wochentag — and am Wochenende ist die Familie zu Hause. 4. The celebrations: Wir feiern Ostern im März oder im April — Ostern ist einmal im Jahr. 5. Your dates keep working: Mein Geburtstag ist im Mai. And the weather runs on: Im November regnet es oft, der Dezember ist dunkel.
pattern.linguist_note: German builds its calendar out of Tag exactly the way English builds out of day: Feiertag, Wochentag, Geburtstag, Freitag. The factory is shared; only the parts are German. English even kept one finished product — Easter — straight from the same Germanic shelf as Ostern.

exercises.prompt: The year's end and its holidays — match each sentence with its reading:

matching_pairs.english: The third of October is a holiday
Easter is in March or in April
matching_pairs.german: Ostern ist im März oder im April

exercises.target_answer: Im November regnet es oft, Der Dezember ist dunkel, Heute ist ein Feiertag, Der 3. Oktober ist ein Feiertag, Ostern ist im März oder im April, Ostern ist einmal im Jahr, Mein Geburtstag ist im Mai
exercises.meaning: the last months, the holiday words, and your dates
exercises.explanation: Everything rides on frames you already own: im + the bare month, ist + ein Feiertag, einmal im Jahr from the frequency lesson. And it is all true — Germany's national holiday really is the 3. Oktober, and Easter really does fall only in März or April.

exercises.prompt: Ostern is the one holiday name English kept. Which English word is its twin — the festival, not the direction?
exercises.meaning: Ostern ↔ Easter: one Germanic name, two languages
exercises.explanation: Ostern and Easter are the same name built on *aust-, 'dawn, east' — the spring festival of the returning light. East is the root's cousin, not the festival: the holiday word is Easter, and German and English both kept it whole.

exercises.prompt: Dezember is Latin decem. Which German number is hiding inside it — the same ancient word as English ten?
exercises.meaning: decem ↔ zehn: the same ancient 'ten', by different roads
exercises.explanation: Latin decem and German zehn both descend from the same Proto-Indo-European 'ten' — and in zehn you can watch the shift do its work: the T hardened to a Z-sound, exactly as in zwei/two and zu/to. Dezember is a later, learned borrowing, so its z is just German's spelling for the Latin c (as in Zentrum). Either way the number never left the name: it was the tenth month of the old Roman count.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the weekday sentence: 'Monday is a weekday'
exercises.explanation: See the compound build itself: Woche + Tag = Wochentag, the same Tag as in Feiertag and Geburtstag. Sonntag and Wochenende wait in the bank — the parts of the week you already own, ready to swap in.

exercises.prompt: Assemble: 'In January and in February it is cold'
exercises.target_answer: Im Januar und im Februar ist es kalt
exercises.meaning: In January and in February it is cold
exercises.explanation: Two time phrases joined by und, then the verb, then es. Swap the pair for any months you own — Im Juli und im August ist es heiß — and the same frame carries the whole year.

summary.outcome: Close the calendar: November and Dezember with their Roman numbers, the Feiertag/Wochentag compounds, and Ostern as the holiday English kept.

use_example.german: Im Dezember feiern wir — Ostern kommt im März oder im April.
use_example.english: In December we celebrate — Easter comes in March or in April.

summary.takeaway: November is novem, Dezember hides zehn (decem), Feiertag and Wochentag are Tag-compounds — and Ostern/Easter is one Germanic name, *aust-, 'dawn, east', kept on both sides of the North Sea.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: Dauer und Termin — how long things last, and the Latin hiding inside the most German verb in the room.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from Kalender III: November, Dezember, Feiertag, Ostern, Wochentag (In January and in February it is cold):
twist.target_answer: Im Januar und im Februar ist es kalt
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Im Januar und im Februar ist es kalt" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of Kalender III: November, Dezember, Feiertag, Ostern, Wochentag without relying on short-term echo.

november.etymology_derivation: Latin loan both languages share: Latin November, inherited via Middle High German. [wiktionary]

dezember.etymology_derivation: Latin loan both languages share: Latin december, inherited via Middle High German. [wiktionary]

feiertag.context_phrase: Heute ist ein Feiertag, alles ist zu.
feiertag.context_translation: Today is a public holiday, everything is closed.
feiertag.etymology_derivation: Feier + Tag — literally celebration day; Tag is the twin of day (d → t). [wiktionary]

ostern.context_translation: We look for Easter eggs at Easter.
ostern.etymology_derivation: From Old High German ōstarūn, from Proto-West Germanic *Austrā; the page compares English Easter — the same Germanic festival name of the dawn-east direction (cf. Osten, east). [wiktionary]

wochentag.context_phrase: Am Wochentag arbeite ich bis fünf.
wochentag.context_translation: On a weekday I work until five.
wochentag.etymology_derivation: Woche + Tag — the exact compound of weekday; both elements are documented twins (week, day). [wiktionary]

feiern.context_translation: We are celebrating a birthday today.
feiern.etymology_derivation: From Old High German firOn, from fira, from Latin feriae (festival days) - the same Latin word that became the English fair, a market held on feast days. [wiktionary][etymonline]

tag.etymology_derivation: Double shift: d → t and y → g.

januar.etymology_derivation: Latin loan both English and German borrowed (via French): Latin Iānuārius. [wiktionary]

februar.etymology_derivation: Latin loan both English and German borrowed (via French): Latin Februārius. [wiktionary]

märz.etymology_derivation: Latin loan both languages share: Latin Martius via Middle High German merze. [wiktionary]

april.etymology_derivation: Latin loan both English and German borrowed (via French): Latin Aprīlis. [wiktionary]

mai.etymology_derivation: Latin loan both languages share: Latin (mensis) Maius via Middle High German meie. [wiktionary]

juli.etymology_derivation: Latin loan both English and German borrowed (via French): Latin Iūlius. [wiktionary]

august.etymology_derivation: Latin loan both English and German borrowed (via French): Latin Augustus. [wiktionary]

oktober.etymology_derivation: Latin loan both languages share: Latin Octōber, from octō 'eight' — the eighth month of the old Roman calendar. [wiktionary]

oft.context_translation: We often play in the park.
oft.etymology_derivation: Old High German ofta — the true twin of English oft/often. [wiktionary]

einmal.context_phrase: Einmal im Jahr fahre ich ans Meer.
einmal.context_translation: Once a year I go to the sea.
einmal.etymology_derivation: ein 'one' + Mal 'time': Middle High German einmāle — literally one-time, hence once. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
